text:
A: Hiya! Can you hear me okay? Sorry, my Wi-Fi's a bit rubbish.
B: Erm, yes, I can hear you. Hi. I'm Kezia.
A: I'm Blerta. I'm in Newcastle. Where are you?
B: Catford. South East London.
A: Oh, nice. I've only been to London twice, like, and both times I got lost at King's Cross. Did you do the puzzle bit at the start? I was so stressed with the timer.
B: Yeah. I didn't like the timer either. I sort of panicked on the third one.
A: Same! I was like, give me a sec, and then it was gone. So what do you do? Are you working or studying?
B: I'm a teaching assistant. SEN, at a primary in Lewisham. I support two children with autism in Year 3.
A: Oh, that's lovely. Do you enjoy it?
B: Yeah, I do. Erm, it's quite routine-based, which I like. I make all their visual timetables, and we use Makaton as well. Do you know Makaton?
A: Yes! Well, a little bit. I'm doing speech and language therapy at uni, second year, so we've done a bit on it. That's so funny, it's like the same area.
B: Oh, really? We get a speech therapist in once a fortnight. She's brilliant.
A: Ah, that's what I want to be. I'm more interested in adults, though, stroke and dementia, because I worked in a care home for six years before uni. So I started late. I'm twenty-seven, and everyone on my course is like nineteen.
B: I don't think that's late. You've got all that experience.
A: That's what my mam says. But sometimes I'm in a lecture at nine o'clock, knackered, and I'm like, what am I doing.
B: I get like that by Thursday. I do four days and by Thursday I'm, you know, done.
A: What's the best bit of it, though? Like, a good day?
B: Erm. There's one boy, I won't say his name, but he's had a now-and-next board for months. That's a board with, this is now, and this is next, with pictures. And he's never touched it himself. And last week he just went over and moved the card on his own, from "carpet" to "snack". And I nearly cried. Sorry, that sounds really small.
A: No, that's not small at all! That's huge. That's him telling you what he wants, on his own.
B: Yeah. The teacher didn't even see it. I logged it, though.
A: Of course you logged it. I saw your bookshelf in the photo, all the folders with labels. I thought, she's definitely organised.
B: They're my resources. I like everything labelled. I've got a planner with colour-coded stickers as well.
A: Oh, I need one of those. My placement notes are okay, but my bedroom's a disaster. What do you do outside work?
B: Church, mostly. I sing in the choir, alto. And Pilates on Tuesdays. Then Sunday dinner at my mum's after church. That's sort of my week.
A: That sounds nice, though. Steady. Ours is tea at six with my mam and dad and my brother, and my dad shouting at the Newcastle match.
B: My dad does that with the England games. My brother as well.
A: It must be a dad thing! I go swimming on Sunday mornings, there's a women-only session and it's cheap. And I volunteer at a conversation café for refugees, practising English.
B: Oh, that's good. Do you speak other languages, then?
A: Albanian. My family's from Kosovo, we came when I was eight. So I translate letters for my aunties and that. It's actually why I want to do assessments in Albanian one day, because loads gets lost when—
